extracted.intended_audience: US patent prosecutors / patent counsel / patent attorneys handling USPTO prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on preparing, filing, and managing 37 C.F.R. § 1.181 petitions asking the USPTO to vacate an incomplete office action and direct issuance of a new complete office action. Focuses on legal standards for completeness, petition content and timing, strategic considerations, and post-filing management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete Office Action Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Office actions must be complete as to the claimed invention's patentability and compliance with statutes, rules, and formalities (35 U.S.C. § 132(a); 37 C.F.R. § 1.104(a)(1); MPEP § 707.07). Final actions have the same completeness requirement (37 C.F.R. § 1.113(b); MPEP §§ 706.07 and 707.07(g)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete actions must address all substantive matters in the application, address all claims, and identify any allowable subject matter. Examiners are instructed to generally avoid piecemeal examination. An action that fails these requirements may be petitionable under 37 C.F.R. § 1.181.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner Duties under MPEP §707.07(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewing and acting on an applicant's response, the examiner must provide clear explanations of actions taken, a complete application file history, and substantive answers to traversed requirements (MPEP § 707.07(f); 37 C.F.R. § 1.112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific duties include: make proper reference to amendments when requirements are traversed and answer their substance; if repeating a rejection, note applicant's argument and answer its substance; if applying a prior rejection to new/amended claims, specifically identify that ground (cite original rejection); if asserted advantages are insufficient, state reasons in the record; if withdrawing a rejection, state reasons and cite relevant pages/lines of applicant remarks. Failure to perform these duties can render an action incomplete and petitionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection-type Specific Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Different rejection categories have particular procedural expectations: prior art rejections (37 C.F.R. § 1.104(c)(2); MPEP §§ 707 and 2143.03) and non-prior art rejections (MPEP § 706.03).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure examiner communications comply with the separate MPEP/regulatory guidance applicable to the rejection type; omissions or misapplication of these specific requirements may support a petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact Prosecution Goals
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO policy favors compact prosecution—reducing the number of actions before allowance or abandonment—and defines minimum information examiners must provide to facilitate prompt, complete examination (MPEP §§ 2103(I) and 2173.06).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compact prosecution is both a procedural expectation and a quality objective. While the examiner count system incentivizes compact prosecution, it can also incentivize shortcuts that reduce examination quality. Applicants should use procedural mechanisms (clear responses, interviews, RCEs, appeals, petitions) to pursue compact, high-quality prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of an Incomplete Office Action (petitionable)
rubrics_metrics.description: An incomplete office action is an action not complete as to all substantive matters (37 C.F.R. § 1.104(b); MPEP § 707.07), typically when the office action ignores or fails to address pending claims or applicant arguments/evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incomplete actions commonly occur as second/subsequent actions that fail to address arguments or amendments traversing a rejection. Both non-final and final actions can be incomplete. The challenged action must be procedurally incomplete (e.g., ignoring at least one claim or at least one argument relevant to a maintained rejection) to be petitionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a Petition Is Inappropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition under § 1.181 is inappropriate to resolve substantive disagreements with the examiner; it is only for procedural incompleteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not petition if the examiner has examined all claims and provided some substantive response. Petitioning on meritorious substantive disputes risks denial and may harm the applicant-examiner relationship; appeals are the correct route for substantive disagreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition Requirements (content and timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A § 1.181 petition must contain a statement of facts, the points to be reviewed (argument), and the action requested, must be filed within two months of the office action, and does not require a fee (37 C.F.R. § 1.181(b); MPEP § 1002).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File as soon as possible and no later than two months after the office action date. Direct the petition to the relevant Technology Center Group Director. Patent Center is the preferred filing method even though it lacks an ePetition form for this petition type. Early filing maximizes chance of favorable processing before response deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting the Petition: Structure and Emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: The petition should be short and structured—Introduction, Facts, Argument, Request for Relief—and should focus on demonstrating the challenged office action is facially incomplete while expressly avoiding substantive review of rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduction should request Group Director find the action incomplete and instruct issuance of a new complete office action; state petition is not seeking review on merits. Facts should summarize the applicant's most recent filing and the office action omissions with page citations. Argument should cite the relevant statute/regulation/MPEP authorities (notably MPEP § 707.07(f)) and apply completeness requirements to demonstrated omissions. Request for Relief should ask withdrawal of the challenged office action and instruction to the examiner to issue a new complete office action examining all claims and addressing all remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request for Relief Content
rubrics_metrics.description: The petition's request should ask that the current office action be withdrawn and that the Group Director instruct the examiner to issue a new complete office action that examines all claims and fully addresses all applicant remarks and arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A granted petition usually results in vacating the challenged action and issuance of a replacement office action with a shortened statutory response time; the replacement may be non-final or final. A grant often results in some patent term adjustment (PTA) accrual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic Considerations Before Filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate likelihood of petition success on the merits, petition timing and pendency risks, prosecution objectives and priorities, practical impact on allowance prospects, and the applicant-examiner relationship; note that the petition requires no fee and is relatively easy to prepare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve petitions for clear cases of incompleteness, especially when allowance may turn on the ignored argument. Consider pairing petitions with examiner interviews or requests to withdraw finality. Balance benefits (corrected action, PTA, saved costs) against potential examiner backlash and petition pendency risks. Early identification of incompleteness in attorney workflow is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition Timing and Pendency Risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions must be filed within two months and do not toll the office action response period (37 C.F.R. § 1.181(f); MPEP § 1002). USPTO petition processing delays often force applicants to file responses (RCE or appeal) to preserve rights, which can render petitions moot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data indicate about 121 days of processing as a threshold for unreasonable delay; petitions delayed beyond that are often dismissed as moot because applicants had to act to preserve the application. File petitions early, track pendency, and be prepared to take preservation steps if the petition decision is delayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing the Petition After Filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Docket and actively follow up on the petition: call the Petitions Office two months after filing and the Ombudsman if no decision in three months; consider examiner interviews and seeking reconsideration after dismissal where practical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active monitoring and prompt follow-up increase likelihood of a timely decision. Requesting an examiner interview and filing a concurrent request to withdraw finality can be coordinated with a petition. If dismissed, call the USPTO official who signed the decision to seek expedited reconsideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential Outcomes, Usage, and Statistical Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical data (2018–2022) show low usage of complete-office-action petitions (fewer than 100 filings), high grant rates on the merits, but a significant portion dismissed—often due to petitions seeking relief on substantive issues or USPTO processing delays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Underutilization likely reflects lack of awareness and workflow timing. Recognize dismissal drivers (petitioning substantive issues; USPTO delay causing response deadline lapse) and plan petition timing and follow-up accordingly to avoid mootness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting on a Denied Petition
rubrics_metrics.description: If the petition is denied, the applicant must still file an office action response by the original six-month statutory deadline; the applicant may seek reconsideration or, in theory, file a writ of mandamus though it is generally impractical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File the response by the statutory deadline. To expedite reconsideration, contact the USPTO official who signed the petition decision. Recognize practical limitations of post-denial remedies due to timing and cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing Examiner Relationship and Interview Strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing a petition spotlights the application and may affect the examiner relationship positively or negatively; interview requests should be granted when reasonable (MPEP § 713.01).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider pairing a strong petition with an examiner interview to convert attention into cooperative prosecution. Be aware petitions may create negative attention for the examiner, which can motivate resolution but also risk examiner displeasure; weigh this when deciding whether to petition.
